messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
We are preparing a vehicle for a club launch. Two-motor cluster, D motors or smaller. Build me something for about 95 m. I'd like it to land under 18 ft/s. Please provide the full design.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: two motors in a cluster (fixed count). Each motor is class D or smaller. Apogee about 95 m, so within 5%, roughly 90 to 100 m. Landing under 18 ft/s: 18 * 0.3048 = 5.49 m/s maximum. Wind, rail and site are not stated, so 2 m/s, a 1.5 m rail, vertical, sea level. Single stage. One parachute.
2. Feasibility: 95 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 95) = 43 m/s. Two D motors are about 30 N*s together, which on a light rocket overshoots 95 m, and two C motors may not lift a fat airframe at 3:1. I need both classes before I choose.

2. Feasibility: two D12 motors would be 16.8 * 2 = 33.6 N*s, about twice the impulse a 95 m flight wants. Two C6 motors are only 4.8 * 2 = 9.6 N of average thrust, so a rocket heavy enough to stay near 95 m would fall under a 3:1 thrust-to-weight. Two C11 motors are 8.8 * 2 = 17.6 N*s and 11.3 * 2 = 22.6 N, still class C, with 3, 5 and 7 s delays. That is the cluster that can both lift and stay low. They are 24 mm, so the two mounts need a tube wider than about 52 mm.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.32 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 22.6 / (0.32 * 9.81) = 7.20. Rail acceleration (22.6 - 3.14) / 0.32 = 60.8 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 60.8 * 1.5) = 13.5 m/s on average thrust. The C11 spikes to 21.7 N each, so the real exit speed should clear 15 m/s. Descent mass 0.32 - 0.024 = 0.296 kg. At 4.5 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.296 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.5^2) = 0.293 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.293 / 3.1416) = 0.611 m. A 0.70 m chute stays under 5.49 m/s. Burn is only 0.78 s, so a 5 s delay ejects near 6 s, about right for a short hop.
4. Draft: 66 mm cardboard tube, 0.45 m long, small ogive nose, four balsa fins, a two-motor 24 mm cluster of C11-5. One chute on ejection. Default wind and a 1.5 m rail.

4. Check: the simulator gives 172.0 m. The target is 95 m, and (172.0 - 95) / 95 = 0.811, so it is 81% high, well outside the 5% band. Margin is 0.48 cal, under 1.0, and 0.48 cal through the burn. Landing 3.2 m/s is under 5.49. Rail exit 20.2 m/s and thrust-to-weight 10.4 pass. Liftoff mass is 0.223 kg, well under my 0.32 kg guess, which is why it climbed. Ejection at 5.8 s matches apogee at 5.76 s, so the delay is right. The cluster did light both motors: total impulse 17.6 N*s.
5. Fix: 172.0 m is the altitude miss and 0.48 cal is the stability miss. Both come from a light tail-heavy rocket, so one nose weight attacks both. Adding 0.15 kg at the top of the tube. That is 0.15 / 0.223 = 0.673 of the current liftoff mass, enough to matter, and it pulls the CG forward. Motors, tube and fins stay put.

4. Check: the simulator gives 86.3 m. That is under the 95 m target: (95 - 86.3) / 95 = 0.0916, about 9% low, outside the 5% band. The nose weight overshot. Everything else passes. Margin is 1.89 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Landing 4.3 m/s is under 5.49. Rail exit 17.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.2. Ejection at 5.8 s is after apogee at 4.47 s, so the altitude is the coast, not a premature chute.
5. Fix: 86.3 m is the miss. The 0.15 kg weight took the rocket from 172.0 m to 86.3 m, and 95 sits between them. Cutting the weight from 0.15 kg to 0.13 kg puts back 0.15 - 0.13 = 0.02 kg of the climb. Margin is 1.89 cal, so losing a little nose mass will not drop it through 1 cal. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: the simulator gives 94.9 m. Against 95 m that is 95 - 94.9 = 0.1 m, inside the 5% band. Landing is 4.1 m/s, under 5.49. Rail exit 17.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.5, margin 1.77 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Two C11 motors, total impulse 17.6 N*s, both under class D. The chute opens at 5.8 s, just after apogee at 4.68 s.
5. Fix: no further change; altitude, landing and margin all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 94.9 m is close to the middle of the band, but it is there because of 0.13 kg of nose weight on a 0.353 kg rocket. A lighter build climbs back toward the 172 m the bare airframe flew. Weigh it. The chute Cd is a model value; 4.1 m/s has room under 5.49 m/s. Drift at 2 m/s was only 32 m.
messages.content:
A two-motor cluster of Estes C11-5 motors in a 66 mm cardboard tube, with 0.13 kg of nose weight and a 0.70 m chute.
The simulator gives 94.9 m, about the 95 m target, 1.77 cal of margin, and a 4.1 m/s landing under the 5.49 m/s limit.
